title: Chapter 28
paragraphs: Levin was insufferably bored that evening with the ladies; he had been stirred as never before by the thought that the dissatisfaction he was feeling with his way of running his estate wasn't a one-off case, but the general state of things in Russia — that working out some relationship between laborers and the soil where they would actually work, as with the peasant he had met on the road to the Sviazhskys', was not a dream but a problem that had to be solved. And it seemed to him the problem could be solved — and that he was the one who ought to try to solve it.

After saying good night to the ladies and promising to stay through the next day so as to ride out with them to see an interesting ruin in the crown forest, Levin went, before turning in, into his host's study to pick up the books on the labor question that Sviazhsky had offered him. Sviazhsky's study was a huge room, walled in by bookcases, with two tables — one a heavy writing-table set in the middle of the room, the other a round table covered with the latest issues of reviews and journals in various languages, arranged like the rays of a star around the lamp. On the writing-table stood a set of drawers labeled in gold lettering and stuffed with papers of every sort.
Sviazhsky pulled out the books and dropped into a rocking chair.
"What are you looking at there?" he said to Levin, who was standing at the round table flipping through the reviews.

"Oh, yes — there's a very interesting article in there," Sviazhsky said of the review Levin was holding. "It seems," he went on with eager interest, "that Friedrich wasn't actually the one chiefly responsible for the partition of Poland. It's been proved..."

And with his usual clarity, he summed up the new, very important, very interesting revelations. Even though Levin was absorbed at that moment by his ideas about the land, he wondered, as he listened to Sviazhsky: "What is there inside this man? And why, of all things, is he interested in the partition of Poland?" When Sviazhsky had finished, Levin couldn't help asking, "Well — and so what?" But there was no "so what." It was simply interesting that things had been shown to be such and such. And Sviazhsky offered no explanation, and saw no need to explain why it was interesting to him.
"Yes — but I was very interested by your irritable neighbor," Levin said with a sigh. "He's a sharp fellow, and a lot of what he said was true."
"Oh, come on! An incurable defender of serfdom at heart, like all of them!" Sviazhsky said.
"Whose marshal you happen to be."
"Yes — only I marshal them in the opposite direction," Sviazhsky said, laughing.

"Here's what really interests me," Levin said. "He's right that our system — rational farming — doesn't answer, and the only thing that does answer is the money-lender approach, like the meek-looking gentleman's, or the simplest possible setup... Whose fault is it?"
"Ours, of course. Besides, it isn't true that it doesn't answer. It answers with Vassiltchikov."
"A factory..."

"But really I don't know what surprises you. The people are at such a low stage of rational and moral development that obviously they're bound to resist anything that's foreign to them. In Europe, a rational system works because the people are educated; therefore we must educate our people — that's all."
"But how do we educate the people?"
"To educate the people, three things are needed: schools, and schools, and schools."
"But you said yourself that the people are at such a low stage of material development — what good will schools do for that?"

"You know, you remind me of the story about the advice given to the sick man — try a purgative. Tried it: worse. Try leeches. Tried them: worse. Well, then, nothing left but prayer. Tried it: worse. That's just how it is with us. I say political economy; you say — worse. I say socialism: worse. Education: worse."
"But how do schools help?"
"They give the peasant new wants."

"Well, that's something I've never understood," Levin shot back. "In what way are schools going to help the people improve their material position? You say schools and education will give them new wants. So much the worse — since they won't be in any position to satisfy them. And how knowing addition and subtraction and the catechism is going to improve their material condition, I've never been able to work out. The other evening I met a peasant woman with a little baby and asked her where she was going. She said she was going to the wise woman; her boy had screaming fits, so she was taking him to be treated. I asked, 'Well, and how does the wise woman cure screaming fits?' 'She puts the child on the hen-roost and says a charm over him...'"
"There — you're saying it yourself! What's needed to keep her from taking her child to the hen-roost to cure his screaming fits is exactly..." Sviazhsky said, smiling good-humoredly.

"Oh, no!" Levin said, irritated. "That cure was just a comparison — for the cure of treating the people with schools. The people are poor and ignorant — we see that as surely as the peasant woman sees that her baby is ill, because it's screaming. But how this trouble of poverty and ignorance is going to be cured by schools is as incomprehensible as how the hen-roost cures the screaming. What has to be cured is whatever is making him poor."

"Well, on that point at least you're in agreement with Spencer — whom you so dislike. He says the same thing — that education may follow from greater prosperity and comfort, from more frequent washing, as he puts it, but not from being able to read and write..."

"Well, then, I'm very glad — or rather very sorry — to be in agreement with Spencer; but I've known it a long time. Schools can do no good; what will do good is an economic arrangement in which the people become wealthier, get more leisure — and then there will be schools."
"Still, all over Europe schools are obligatory now."
"And how far do you yourself agree with Spencer on the question?" Levin asked.
But there was a glint of alarm in Sviazhsky's eyes, and he smiled and said:
"No — that screaming story is positively priceless! Did you really hear it yourself?"

Levin saw he was never going to find the connection between this man's life and his ideas. Plainly he didn't care in the least what his line of reasoning led him to; all he wanted was the process of reasoning itself. And he didn't like it when that process backed him into a corner. That was the one thing he disliked, and he steered around it by switching the conversation to something pleasant and entertaining.

All the impressions of the day — starting with the impression made by the old peasant, which served as a sort of foundation for everything else — threw Levin into violent excitement. This dear, decent Sviazhsky, keeping a stock of ideas in reserve for purely social uses, plainly having some other principles hidden away from Levin, while with the crowd, whose name is legion, he was shaping public opinion with ideas he didn't himself share; that hot-tempered country gentleman, perfectly correct in the conclusions life had hammered into him, but wrong in his bitterness against a whole class — and the best class in Russia at that; his own dissatisfaction with the work he had been doing, and the vague hope of finding a remedy for all of it — all of it blended into a sense of inward churning and an anticipation of some solution very close at hand.

Left alone in the room they had given him, lying on a spring mattress that yielded unexpectedly under every movement of his arm or leg, Levin couldn't fall asleep for a long while. Not a single one of Sviazhsky's lines, however clever, had really interested him; but the irascible landowner's conclusions deserved a careful look. Levin couldn't help running back over every word the man had said, and revising in his head his own replies.

"Yes, what I should have said to him was — you say our farming doesn't work because the peasant hates improvements, and they have to be forced on him from above. If no system of farming worked at all without those improvements, you'd be entirely right. But the one system that does work is the one where the laborer is working in accordance with his own habits, just like the old peasant's land on the way here. Your dissatisfaction and ours with the existing system shows that either we are to blame or the laborers are. We've gone on our way — the European way — for a long time without ever asking ourselves about the qualities of our labor force. Let's try looking at the labor force not as some abstract force but as the _Russian peasant_ with his own instincts, and we'll arrange our farming accordingly. Imagine, I ought to have said to him, that you have the same setup the old peasant has, that you've found a way to make your laborers take an interest in the success of the work, and that you've found a happy middle ground in the kind of improvements they'll accept — and you'll get, without exhausting the soil, two or three times the yield you got before. Divide it in halves, give half as the laborers' share; the surplus left to you will be greater, and the laborers' share will be greater too. And to make this work, one has to lower the standard of farming and get the laborers interested in its success. How to do that? — that's a matter of detail; but it can be done, no doubt about it."

The idea threw Levin into a great state of excitement. He didn't sleep half the night, working out in detail how to put the idea into practice. He hadn't planned to leave the next day, but now he was determined to head home early in the morning. Besides, the sister-in-law with her low-cut bodice stirred in him a feeling close to shame and remorse, as though he had committed some thoroughly base act. Most important of all — he had to get back without delay: he would have to hurry to put his new plan to the peasants before the sowing of the winter wheat, so that the sowing could be done on the new footing. He had made up his mind to overhaul his whole system.
